content: The cMYP (comprehensive Multi-Year Plan) is a critical tool for program and resource planning. It is also essential for advocacy efforts directed at the Ministry of Health, Ministry of Finance, international donors, and development partners to support the expansion and improvement of immunization programs. Financial sustainability strategies should form the foundation of advocacy for the program. Advocacy efforts must be aligned with strategies designed to achieve the program’s financial sustainability objectives. In many cases, stakeholders involved in the immunization program will also serve as target audiences for advocacy messages. During the development of the cMYP, there are numerous opportunities for both formal and informal interactions with stakeholders. To monitor and evaluate the financial sustainability of the program, it is recommended to select a small number of indicators and related targets. These indicators and targets should assess the reliability, efficiency, adequacy, and self-sufficiency of financial resources. A list of potential indicators is provided in Annex 11, but countries may also choose other indicators tailored to their specific circumstances. Reliability refers to the availability of financial resources allocated for the program at the right time and place. Reliability can fail when budgetary allocations are made but funds are not released when needed. An example of a reliability indicator could be the proportion of local government allocations for immunization that are actually expended. A target might be that 90% or more of local government allocations for immunization program inputs are expended during the first two years of the cMYP, increasing to 95% or more during the last three years. Efficiency is defined as achieving the maximum output for a given level of expenditure. An example of an efficiency indicator could be the vaccine wastage rate, with a target of reducing the wastage rate by two percentage points per year to achieve a rate 10 percentage points lower than the baseline by the end of the cMYP. Adequacy of resources means that efforts to mobilize financing from national and external sources are successful in securing the funding needed to achieve program objectives. An example of an adequacy indicator could be sub-national government spending on per diems for outreach and community mobilization activities. A target might be that sub-national governments mobilize at least 90% of the funds planned for outreach and community mobilization in the first year of the cMYP. Self-sufficiency is the ultimate goal of financial sustainability for the immunization program. As the program expands and improves, national contributions to cover program costs must increase to move toward self-sufficiency. Once the cMYP development stage is complete, the next step is to implement the plan, which includes dissemination, implementation, and monitoring. Dissemination involves ensuring that the plan is approved and endorsed by higher levels of the national structure, integrating its main goals and targets into the Health Sector Plan, and consulting with the Ministry of Health and Ministry of Finance to ensure financing is incorporated into multi-year funding commitments. The plan should be presented and discussed with the ICC (Interagency Coordinating Committee), partners, and broader health-sector forums. In some contexts, meetings with parliamentarians or political leaders may be convened to secure their commitment to the immunization program. The plan should also be disseminated to all sub-national levels and other stakeholders involved in the planning process. Public forums involving civil society, professional associations, academia, the private sector, and the media can be established to communicate the main goals and targets of the cMYP. Annual planning is a critical component of implementation. Each year, an activity plan or work plan should be prepared for the upcoming year, ideally involving sub-national levels during an annual review and planning meeting. The development of the annual plan should be synchronized with the national planning process and involve key stakeholders. In countries with an annual review process at the sub-national level, the review of the national immunization program and the cMYP should be integrated into this process. This integration broadens discussions on the implementation of the cMYP and ensures appropriate linkages with the multi-year plan. For subsequent years, a situation analysis should be conducted to revise activities and make them more relevant. The situation analysis should be updated using the monitoring and evaluation framework, with indicators disaggregated to the lowest geographic level possible to identify areas of underperformance in coverage, equity of access, surveillance, cold-chain logistics, or other technical components of the immunization system. This analysis can guide national and sub-national health systems and program planners in updating annual work plans and reallocating resources based on evidence of health and program needs. Integration and consolidation of activities are also essential for implementation. Integration involves conducting joint activities between immunization and other health priorities, as indicated in the national health plan. This may include joint planning and resource sharing. Consolidation aims to identify common problems in the immunization system and share responsibilities for corrective actions. For example, obstacles to polio eradication may also affect measles mortality reduction, neonatal tetanus elimination, and routine immunization coverage. Teams can work together to address these issues. Prioritization of activities is necessary to address gaps in the immunization system, particularly in underserved geographic areas. District and sub-district level data should be analyzed to select priority districts and communities. Coverage assessments and mapping should be conducted to identify areas of underperformance or low coverage. If additional resources are needed to reach underserved areas, this should be discussed during the planning process to ensure budget estimates reflect actual needs and sufficient funds can be generated. At the end of each year or quarter, an immunization planning and review meeting should be conducted with national and sub-national immunization managers, relevant departments, and partner agencies. These meetings provide an opportunity to evaluate the previous annual work plan, discuss achievements and challenges, and develop the upcoming annual work plan based on available data and resources. Stakeholders in immunization service delivery, including local authorities, surveillance staff, the private sector, and NGOs, should also participate in the review and planning process. The cMYP development process involves seven planning steps, which align with the seven components of the immunization system and the seven health system building blocks. Planning is an ongoing, cyclical process that uses data, information, and dialogue to adapt to changing immunization and health system contexts. The ultimate goal is to ensure that the cMYP is effectively implemented, monitored, and continuously improved to achieve immunization program objectives.
